item.title: In the near term, I'm far more bullish on the '3D portal' means of making flatscreen games work in VR than shoddy conver
item.dc:creator: benz145
item.content:encoded:
In the near term, I'm far more bullish on the '3D portal' means of making flatscreen games work in VR than shoddy conversations which end up with a 'VR-compatible' version of the game that's more work and less fun (and for many people, uncomfortable) to play in a headset than on a flatscreen.
This is a matter of pragmatism. If every flatscreen game could get the amount of time and investment needed to be thoroughly redesigned to be *great* in VR, then I'd obviously prefer that. The reality is that that's a time consuming, expensive, and very challenging to do right for 95% of games, and the ROI simply isn't there for the developer.
And for anyone who says "isn't this just a 3D monitor?" ... there is a qualitative difference between a portal into a game with 6DOF tracking and zero crosstalk than anything you've seen from a 3D monitor or even 3D movie. It's a much more immersive experience.

item.title: Well, I’m testing CoreCLR right now with Unity 7 Alpha!
item.dc:creator: Dilmerv
item.content:encoded:
Well, I’m testing CoreCLR right now with Unity 7 Alpha!
Below are the steps to enable it, but looks like it is set by default in Unity 7 Alpha.
Edit → Project Settings → Player → Other Settings → Configuration → Scripting Backend → CoreCLR.
📌 Here're a few great things about it:
- Modern JIT compiler to optimize C# execution. - Generational garbage collection for managing memory. - Better debugging with standard .NET tools. - .NET 10 and C# 14 support planned for future updates.
📊 Few community benchmarks with Unity 6.7’s experimental desktop player (from Unity forums):
- C# CPU path tracing, single thread: 17.1× speedup vs Mono and 2.49× vs IL2CPP. - C# CPU path tracing, multiple threads: 17.85× speedup vs Mono and 2.81× vs IL2CPP. - Boat Attack: ~10% lower average frame time vs Mono in a quick single-run test. - Happy Harvest: ~15% lower average frame time vs Mono in a quick single-run test.
In summary: It’s supposed to be very, very fast when you hit Play in Unity. I’m testing that right now with the Meta XR SDKs!

item.title: About a year and a half ago, I built a few demos with microgestures, and they’re extremely relevant now with Meta VR Gla
item.dc:creator: Dilmerv
item.content:encoded:
About a year and a half ago, I built a few demos with microgestures, and they’re extremely relevant now with Meta VR Glasses! These are small, low-effort thumb movements that let you trigger actions, navigate content, and even move through VR without controllers or large hand movements. 🙌
- Thumb tap and double tap for contextual actions and shortcuts - Swipe left, right, up, or down for directional input - Navigate UI and content almost like using a tiny D-pad with your thumb - Combine microgestures with gaze for low-effort targeting and interactions - Use them for locomotion, paging, media controls, teleportation, and other contextual actions
These are a few prototypes I built to test these features. Additionally, the gaze features that will be available in the future will further enhance this functionality. https://x.com/Dilmerv/status/2107861768072729059/photo/1

item.title: XREAL Aura starts from $1,279. I guess the price has been carefully studied so as not to be more than Meta VR Glasses. E
item.dc:creator: SkarredGhost

item.title: All, Unity 7 alpha is now available! 🚀
item.dc:creator: Dilmerv
item.content:encoded:
All, Unity 7 alpha is now available! 🚀
This release brings a CoreCLR-powered Editor, a new script-reloading workflow, and several XR rendering improvements. It’s an early step toward Unity’s modern .NET foundation, with C# 14 and .NET 10 support in the Editor planned for later.
- CoreCLR replaces Mono in the Editor, laying the foundation for modern .NET support.
- A new code-reloading system uses AssemblyLoadContext, with bigger iteration-speed improvements planned for future releases.
- Temporal Pixel Synthesis support has been added for XR rendering.
- XR Quad Views optimizations reduce CPU and GPU work by reusing rendering data and reducing redundant geometry rendering.
- IL2CPP improvements eliminate unnecessary boxing and memory allocations in several common value-type operations.
📌 For more details about this version check out the Unity discussion https://discussions.unity.com/t/unity-7-0-alpha-is-now-available/1738310

item.title: One of my favorite features on Quest & 🕶️ Meta VR Glasses is passthrough, which opens up so many possibilities for Mixed
item.dc:creator: Dilmerv
item.content:encoded:
One of my favorite features on Quest & 🕶️ Meta VR Glasses is passthrough, which opens up so many possibilities for Mixed Reality experiences!
To me, this is an incredibly interesting area to explore. Instead of building an experience that simply floats in the user’s space, think about how you can turn their physical world into a canvas or playground. How can your game or app understand, utilize, and transform the area around them?
📌 Here're a few areas to explore...
- Use passthrough as a 360-degree background - Place virtual content on physical walls, floors, and tables - Create windows and portals between physical and virtual worlds - Use lighting, dimming, and color to guide the user’s attention - Blend smoothly between Mixed Reality and fully immersive VR - Combine passthrough with scene understanding to make virtual objects interact with the real environment
Combine passthrough with scene understanding to make virtual objects interact naturally with physical surfaces. Characters can walk across your walls, floors, and tables, turning the entire room into a canvas for your experience. https://x.com/Dilmerv/status/2107546956998574419/video/1
If your app frequently switches between passthrough and fully immersive VR, provide an easily accessible toggle in the main or pause menu. Use smooth blending between the two modes, since sudden transitions can feel overwhelming or uncomfortable. https://x.com/Dilmerv/status/2107546958915326353/photo/1
To learn more about Mixed Reality and passthrough best practices, check out this guide. It goes into much more detail about how these features work and how to use them effectively 👇 https://developers.meta.com/vr/design/mr-design-passthrough/

item.title: Here’s a question I’ve been getting a lot recently: How do you move around in VR without controllers? 🙌
item.dc:creator: Dilmerv
item.content:encoded:
Here’s a question I’ve been getting a lot recently: How do you move around in VR without controllers? 🙌
𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻. It’s simply how we move through a virtual world, even when our physical space is limited.
For hands-first experiences on Meta VR Glasses, we can combine hand movements with microgestures to move, turn, crouch, and more!
A single thumb tap while your hand is idle, rather than aiming at UI, activates the locomotion method selected in your app’s preferences.
Let’s look at Walkingsticks, Telepath, and the familiar Teleport 👇
Walkingsticks 🚶
This one is pretty cool: swing your hands/arms to walk through the virtual world!
Here’s how the controls work:
- Walk: Swing your hands/arms. - Snap turn: Swipe your right thumb left/right. - Step: Swipe your left thumb left/right/up/down. - Crouch: Swipe your right thumb down. - Jump: Move both hands down as if pushing off the ground.
Your arm movements become part of how you navigate!
Telepath 👀
Pick where you want to go, then walk there virtually. Move your arm to aim at a destination and tap to start moving!
- Walk to a destination: Aim with your arm and tap. - Snap turn: Swipe your right thumb left/right. - Step: Swipe your left thumb left/right/up/down. - Crouch: Swipe your right thumb down. - Jump: Swipe your right thumb up.
The key difference from teleporting is that you travel through the space to reach your destination.
Teleport 🙌
This is probably the one most of you already know! Aim at where you want to go, then tap to teleport there.
- Teleport: Aim with your arm and tap. - Snap turn: Swipe your right thumb left/right. - Step: Swipe your left thumb left/right/up/down. - Crouch: Swipe your right thumb down.
One thing for devs to keep in mind: current microgestures recognize discrete inputs, not a continuous thumbstick-style input.
Which of these would you use in your hands-first game or app? 👇

item.title: Here’s an example of how I use the XR Simulator to test ISDK Hand Grab Poses! It works very well, and I can now connect
item.dc:creator: Dilmerv
item.content:encoded:
Here’s an example of how I use the XR Simulator to test ISDK Hand Grab Poses! It works very well, and I can now connect Meta XR Operator to my agent and have it iterate through a lot of different models to evaluate the accuracy of the grab poses, or at least assign them a quality score. I use WASD to move around and the mouse to pan or rotate.
The hand grab poses shown here were generated by the new tool I have been building, so no more manual creation of poses. However, the system allows you to tweak joints if needed. But having these poses authored by a tool can save a lot of time.
